title: Scientists Uncover Why Men's Prostates Grow Larger With Age, New Study Reveals
body:
A team of researchers has identified a previously unrecognised cell subtype within the human prostate that appears to drive the organ’s gradual enlargement with age, a condition known medically as benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH). The discovery, made through a combination of single‑cell RNA sequencing and advanced tissue‑mapping techniques, could reshape the way clinicians understand and eventually treat a disorder that affects up to half of men over 60 and is a leading cause of urinary problems worldwide.

The investigators, based at a leading university’s department of urology and collaborating biotech firms, isolated prostate tissue from donors ranging in age from 20 to 80 years. By analysing the gene‑expression profiles of thousands of individual cells, they uncovered a distinct population of stromal cells—dubbed “fibro‑myoid progenitors”—that proliferate markedly in older specimens. Unlike the well‑characterised smooth‑muscle cells that form the prostate’s supportive framework, these progenitors express a unique set of signaling molecules, including high levels of fibroblast growth factor 7 (FGF7) and transforming growth factor‑beta (TGF‑β) isoforms, which together appear to stimulate surrounding epithelial cells to multiply and secrete additional extracellular matrix.

Benign prostatic hyperplasia has long been attributed to a complex interplay of hormonal changes, inflammation, and age‑related tissue remodeling, but the precise cellular mechanisms have remained elusive. Traditional histological studies identified an overall increase in stromal and epithelial cell numbers, yet could not pinpoint which cell types were the primary drivers. The new findings suggest that the fibro‑myoid progenitors act as a sort of “master switch,” orchestrating the hyperplastic response by releasing growth‑promoting cues that cause the gland’s fibromuscular stroma to expand. This insight explains why BPH tends to progress slowly over decades, mirroring the gradual accumulation of these progenitor cells.

The implications for treatment are significant. Current medical options—alpha‑blockers, 5‑alpha‑reductase inhibitors, and minimally invasive surgical procedures—focus on relieving urinary symptoms or shrinking the gland indirectly, often with side effects such as sexual dysfunction or orthostatic hypotension. Targeting the newly identified progenitor cells could allow for more precise interventions that halt or reverse tissue overgrowth at its source. The research team has already begun screening small‑molecule inhibitors that block FGF7 signaling, showing promising reductions in cell proliferation in laboratory cultures. If these compounds prove effective in animal models, they could pave the way for a new class of BPH therapeutics that avoid the drawbacks of existing drugs.

Experts not involved in the study caution that translating cellular discoveries into clinical practice will require extensive validation. Dr. Elena Martinez, a urologist at a major teaching hospital, notes that BPH is a heterogeneous condition, with some men experiencing rapid growth while others remain asymptomatic for life. “Understanding whether fibro‑myoid progenitors are the dominant factor across all patient sub‑groups, or whether they interact with other pathways like androgen metabolism, will be essential before we can develop targeted therapies,” she said.

Nevertheless, the identification of a discrete cell subtype responsible for prostate enlargement marks a milestone in urological research. By illuminating the cellular choreography behind a condition that imposes a substantial burden on health systems and quality of life, the study opens a pathway toward more personalized, mechanism‑based treatments. As further investigations explore how these progenitor cells are regulated—and whether lifestyle factors such as diet, exercise, or inflammation influence their activity—men worldwide may soon benefit from therapies that keep the prostate in check without compromising overall wellbeing.
